Do you think that Steven Spielberg would have had the career he's had without John Williams?

I know it may seem blasphemous to even consider with Spielberg being one of the most frequently discussed filmmakers when it comes to the best directors of all time, but I can't help but wonder how much of Spielberg's career success is due to his pairing with composer John Williams. Granted, Spielberg has enormous talent as a director but I honestly can't picture any of his great movies (Jaws, Close Encounters, Indiana Jones, Jurassic Park, E.T.) without hearing Williams' music in my head. Jaws in particular works so successfully due to it's music, the fact that this was Spielberg's breakout success just makes me wonder how the film would have landed without it's iconic score. And granted, Williams had already produced several soundtracks prior to working on Jaws, so maybe they just brought out the best in one another and it's truly hard to separate which component benefited more from their collaboration. Like Danny Elfman and Tim Burton or in the sports world Joe Montana and Jerry Rice. Just thought it was an interesting conversation worth having.

Watched 'Greyhound' last night.

What a fantastic movie. I'm on a bit of a submarine binge at the moment and thought i'd give this a watch and was very impressed. Action all the way through and granted, there was an element of hollywood-esque unrealism to some of the action, but overall really good.

The atlantic war is a real untapped resources for war movies in my opinion. Aside from Das Boot, I can't really think of anything else that warrants a watch. I've thought about watching u-571 but the historical accuracy element puts me off a bit. 

Glad to read a a sequel is being developed.

SCARFACE is too campy to be taken seriously. How can anyone not laugh at Al Pacino's endless screaming and scenery chewing?

I was laughing my ass at most of what was onscreen. It was as if everyone was competing on who overacted the most. Robert Loggia was ridiculous with that Cuban accent and moustache, even the scene where he's pleading for his life is comedy gold with the pay-off, or MIriam Colon playing Pacino's mother (?), even though they look the same age, ranting and raving. Even poor Mary Elizabeth Manstrantion got her one big scene, where she goes from being the normal one to being just as wacko with no explanation. 

The best performance, in my mind, came from Michelle Pfeiffer as Elvira. She seemed to be the only one taking it seriously, adding subtlety to her character, but that only makes Pacino's overacting more obvious when they share scenes together.

Melissa McCarthy didn't live up to the promise of BRIDESMAIDS but SPY is a hilarious comedy that gave Melissa McCarthy the opportunity to finally shine.

It's the only comedy I felt she blew it out of the park. I even think it's better than THE HEAT. It didn't make a lot of money, bummer, but it's funny, it's quick, the jokes land and McCarthy is hilarious, engaging and actually convincing in a part that required her to be a spy. It never poked fun at her weight, mostly, which meant MM could deliver her comedy chops without resorting to fat jokes. 

The best part is that the supporting cast is also terrific. Rose Byrne is a standout. Jason Statham makes fun of his action persona and is a good sport about it. 

And even as a action movie, I thought it worked. If only we got a SPY 2.

Do you think TV shows generally have bigger more loyal fanbases than films?

I know you're all probably sick and tired of this whole debate about movies vs shows, but my question isn't about which of these mediums you like more as they're two seperate things and it all really depends. 

I've noticed recently, especially with shows and movies coming out right now, apart from franchises most movies die out pretty fast and people stop talking about them, whereas TV shows due to their length build bigger fanbases and you see it being discussed amongst fans for a very long time, even shows that aren't that popular. 

I think this is one advantage shows have over movies, and more specifically ones from this century. I'm not talking about cult classics or films released 25-30+ years ago (some even 80 years) that are still in people's mouths to this day, but moreso this century since these past 2 decades have been the golden age of television. 

I see the most popular films from the last 5 years and the most popular shows from the past 5 years and you'd immediately realize there are more shows being talked about than movies. Even take subreddits for example: How many big subreddits dedicated to shows have you seen? Then compare that to how many subreddits dedicated to certain movies, barely any if none apart from franchises. 

Are there any movies you know that have a big loyal fan base which are still talked about? I'm obviously not talking about films from this year.
I think the whole movie is now worthless now. Seems like they are wiping the slate clean.

i guess the counterargument would be F4, Push, The Losers and Cellular aren't leading man action hero roles like Jurassic World, Tomorrow War, Terminal List, etc. F4, Push and The Losers were all part of an ensemble cast and Cellular was much more of a thriller where anyone could've been cast as Evans' character .. rather than him being a hero.

[Looking at his filmography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Chris_Evans_performances) it's probably the second Cpt America and Snowpiercer that are closest to the action hero roles Pratt tries to get. but of course they're outnumbered in Evans' filmography by plenty of dramas, some rom coms, teen movies, thrillers, more lighthearted stuff or ensemble stuff, etc. much more variety+range from evans is what the previous user probably meant, rather than the two being in the same lane.

With all of the discussion on the Sight and Sound poll, how would you have filled out your ballot if given one?

[The results of 2022's Sight and Sound poll ](https://www.bfi.org.uk/news/revealed-results-2022-sight-sound-greatest-films-all-time-poll) were recently released, causing quite a bit of discussion on the results, as ever. With that in mind, I'm curious as to what others might have given as responses if given a chance. The poll consists of ten, unranked, responses to the question: "What are the ten greatest films of all time?"

So, what are, in your opinion, the ten greatest films of all time? I figure if this gets enough responses, I'll compile them into our own version of the poll!

How Do You Reconcile Problematic/Offensive Elements In Your Favorite Older Films?

Before I get attacked for being "woke" or "sjw" and blah blah blah I'd like to clarify that I've always maintained a staunch position of "sometimes older art ages poorly in some ways. AND THAT'S OK."

I believe in acknowledging problematic elements without moralizing about the fans or filmmakers as bad people who need to answer for their crimes, so to speak. 

But despite my stance of "being problematic isn't the end of the world" I find myself taken aback by things in older favorites I never noticed before. 

The new Indy 5 trailer got me excited to watch the originals again. They've always been favorites but I realized I hadn't sat down to watch them through in some time. 

Suffice it to say I was floored to see straight up yellow face in Raiders. A white stunt man with prosthetics made up to look Asian. I've seen Raiders dozens of times yet somehow never noticed until now. 

It threw me for a loop, to be honest. There is also brown face in the film. 

I will always consider Raiders one of my favorite films ever. Temple of Doom, which is more controversial, is my favorite Indy film period. 

But I won't lie that these poorly aged elements aren't something of a sore spot to grudgingly get past. 

I want to make it clear that I'm not talking about "canceling" anything nor am do I want this to devolve into a screed about political correctness and anti-wokeness. 

I want to have an open discussion on how fellow film fans personally reconcile offensive aspects of films they love.

Which sequel is WAY better than the original?

I'm not even talking about stuff like "Terminator 2" being better than the first one - both are good movies.

I mean a case of serious improvement over part one - to mind comes Tommy Wirkolas "Dead Snow 2". While the first one is quite an okay but trashy Nazi zombie flick, the second one is seriously bat shit insane, has an innovative story and really beats the original movie on every level.

What do you think?

'All Quiet on the Western Front' is a golden feather in Netflix's cap

Just saw this yesterday on Netflix and must say it just might be the best Netflix original movie and is one of the best World War movies. It shows you the horror of the War, especially the WW1. I might have cried twice during the movie, the POV is great, plus it is engrossing to see how the negotiations worked out alongside the war.  
Plus, it succeeds alright in giving out the Anti-War message by basing it on a 17-year-old boy who has enrolled in the army just because he did not want to feel left out. The music score is spot on, and the scenes (especially the one where Paul stabs the enemy soldier in the pit) make you want to cry your heart out.

Oh, this one does a great job at showing you the German side of things too, something that was unnecessarily criticized in some of the critic reviews I feel. The film also does great at making you hate the higher-ranking officials by showing a proper contrast in the lives of the soldiers and the major general fuckers.  

Kat deserved a better end than being shot by a 8-year-old chum from the farm but apart from that, it is absolute gold.

Building off of this, but a bit more nuanced:  

Both Evelyn and Joy are experiencing a large amount of chaos as a result of verse jumping repeatedly. Evelyn, having a great more experience dealing with the general malaise of day to day chaos, is able to filter out and hone in on what she believes *her* experience is supposed to be (and tries to nudge other versions of herself towards this).  

Joy, on the other hand, is overwhelmed. Rather than finding a calming center (... like the hole of a bagel...) she is hyperfocused on everything *around* (the bagel) to the point that her sense of self, in any given verse, is distorted and bleeds over to the next: there is no grounding aspect to feel connected to a given moment as she continually experiences everything, everywhere, all at once.  

This is also supported early on in the beginning, when Alpha Waymond states that "verse jumping creates small cracks between you and other versions of yourself. In time, you will learn how to heal these fractures." Evelyn learned how to - Joy did not.

​

Evelyn, by *forcing* them to stay in a specific verse to have direct bits of conversation, can some of the chaos "calm down" enough to have insight as to seek direction within the given moment - and be less distracted by others (or, alternatively, by having that skill be shared so that each verse can co-exist without bleeding through).
